chapter: New York bands and the first records
title: Hammond takes the records to England; Esquire forces release
summary: John Hammond brought copies back from England, leading to record offers for Norvo, Goodman and Mildred, and an Esquire poll forced American release.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: So, I said, 'Okay.' At least I had the pleasure of making it, I told him. And I left. I didn't hear anymore about it. Well it seems that John Hammond, went to visit his sister in England and he brought back -- I forget how many -- he told me a couple times, I might get the number wrong. 20 maybe or 25 of those records. From England and he gave them to his friends. Here in the STates. Different-people.
So, it -- he told me when he came back and then Benny came over to the house in Forest Hills and said this

fella wanted to meet us and he also came back with a commitment for Benny to make some records, for me to make some records, and for Mildred to make some records. So, that's the way I started the first record thing, Benny started his first record thing, and Mildred made that Squeeze Me and those other records that she made.
Yeah. Were they made for an English label, --
They were made for Columbia on -- no Columbia wasn't in business then. It was made -- Columbia was out of business --
Yeah.
-- but I think it went to --
Parlophone --
Parlophone and -- or English Decca, one of those --
Yeah.
And -- so now these records that John Hammond -- if you want to we can go back to John's record dates, you know --
Yeah, well listen did anything ever --
Yes. Now the records came out and was given to these critics and people, like the priest in Boston, and Marshall Sterns and all that --
The original one?
What?
The original IN a Mist?
Yeah, that he brought back.
Yeah.
They weren't out in this country.
No. That's right.

So then a number of critics voted in Esquire the 25 most -- well the most different or influential type -- style records in all jazz. And this, In a Mist and "Dance of the Octopus" was included. So Jack Capp had to put it out.
Well he had --
--He -- that company -- they put it out, they put it out, they finally put it out.
Did he ever talk to you about it?
No. He never mentioned it again, but they put it out.
Isn't that --
I think their first pressing on it was 10,000 or something like that.
Isn't that --
-- Isn't that funny --
A classic in spite of himself.
Yeah. So -- there's nothing against Jack Capp, it's just that he was a businessman --
I know, I know -- yeah.
He just felt the market wasn't ready for that sort of thing --
No.
